seo.title: AI Audio Research | Igor Szuniewicz
seo.description: Bachelor Thesis: Can AI generate sound effects in real-time for video games?

header.title: Can AI Generate Game Audio in Real-Time?
header.description: For my bachelor thesis, I built a system that connects Unity to AI audio models through a Python WebSocket server. I tested whether AI can generate sound effects fast enough for games — and what happens when it can't.

setup.title: What I Tested and Why
setup.intro: Games ship with hundreds of pre-recorded sound files. Every gunshot, footstep and explosion is a WAV file someone recorded in a studio. AI could generate these on the fly — unique every time, adapting to context, no gigabytes of audio assets. The catch is latency. If a sound comes even 100ms late, players notice.
setup.approach: I built a prototype: a Unity game that sends audio requests over WebSocket to a Python server, which calls an AI model and streams the result back. I tested three models — ElevenLabs (cloud API, best quality but inconsistent latency), MMAudio (video-to-audio, adapted for game events, runs locally), and AudioGen (Meta's text-to-audio, most consistent but still slow).

results.title: Measured Latency
results.subtitle: Generation times for each model, compared to what games actually need. Log scale — the differences are that large.

tooltip.elevenlabs: Cloud API. Best quality, but latency varies wildly — 1s to 12s on the same day.
tooltip.mmaudio: Video-to-audio model adapted for game use. Runs locally, 2-5s per sound.
tooltip.audiogen: Meta's text-to-audio. Most consistent at ~3s, but still too slow for real-time.
tooltip.cached: Pre-generated sounds served from memory. 21-55ms delivery time.

elevenlabs.note: Cloud-based, quality depends on server load

mmaudio.note: Local, originally designed for video soundtracks

audiogen.note: Most consistent, but 3s is still 3s too slow

solution.title: Caching as the Actual Solution
solution.story: None of the models came close to real-time. The fastest was still over a second — about 60x too slow for a gunshot. I had added a simple cache early on, just to avoid regenerating the same sound twice. Then I noticed the cache hit times in the server logs: 21-55ms. That's within the acceptable range for games.
solution.insight: The approach shifted from "make AI faster" to "call AI at the right time." Generate sounds during loading screens or quiet moments, store them in a cache, and serve them instantly when the player needs them. When a cached sound is used, the system quietly generates a replacement in the background.

loading.label: Loading Screen
loading.description: AI generates sounds in the background while the player waits

play.label: Player Acts
play.description: Sound plays from cache in under 55ms

refill.label: Background Refill
refill.description: System generates replacement sounds for next time

solution.usecases: This works best for predictable sounds — ambient audio, cutscene effects, gunshots with limited fire rates. It struggles with very frequent events like footsteps, where the cache drains faster than AI can refill it.

closing.conclusion: AI audio isn't ready to replace traditional game sound design. Generation is too slow for real-time use. But with predictive caching, it can supplement it — adding variety and reducing asset file sizes for the right use cases.
closing.reflection: The interesting finding wasn't about any specific model. It was that the problem was architectural, not computational. The technology will keep getting faster, but even today, thinking about when to generate matters more than how fast you generate.

session2.title: Session #2 Findings: The Local AI Reality (Failed)
session2.content: Date: 2025-12-05. We attempted to run MusicGen and AudioLDM2 locally on student hardware (No CUDA). Result: 4-10 seconds latency per sound. Conclusion: Pure local AI is currently unfeasible for twitch-reaction gameplay. We need a faster solution.

session4.title: Session #4 Findings: Stress Testing the Hybrid Model
session4.content:
Date: 2025-12-05. We stressed the new 'Hybrid' architecture (Procedural + Cloud AI). 
- Burst Test: 100 simultaneous requests handled in <200ms.
- Throughput: 2253 generations/sec achieved.
- Latency: 5.02ms (Procedural) vs 2-4s (Cloud).
The hybrid approach is confirmed viable for production.
